issues.display_title: Issue #84: Implement Control Point for Stitch 360
issues.main_description_html:
Demo by developer

WhatsApp.Video.2026-07-17.at.6.26.34.PM.1.mp4

The "Control Point" feature in Stitch 360 (lets a user mark the same spot on two photos so the panorama lines up more accurately) is now actually wired into the photo-stitching process — before this, it was just a UI, the points a user drew were never used.

Done:

  • User can create points from scratch (no need for an automatic alignment pass first)
  • Those points are now actually used when the photos are merged into a panorama
  • Covered by automated tests (18 tests) + 1 real test using actual photos, all passing
  • The photo-stitching engine (pt-stitch) was also updated to the latest version

Still needed:

  • Manual testing in the running app — open the app, mark real points on real photos, run a stitch, check the result looks right. This has not been tried at all yet.
  • The Mac build of the stitching engine hasn't been updated yet (Windows only so far)

PR: #83 (not merged yet, waiting on the manual test above)

issues.display_title: Issue #56: [Epic] Integrate GoThru-PtGui Stitching App Into Main Rust App
issues.main_description_html:
Source

User feedback

Goal

Integrate the standalone GoThru-PtGui stitching Rust app (built with Fable 5, currently usable/beta) into the main Photo Studio Rust app.
https://github.com/GoThruMedia/GoThru-PtGui

Key consideration

The author will keep updating the standalone GoThru-PtGui repo. Integration must account for ongoing upstream changes — decide the integration strategy:

  • Vendor as a git submodule / path dependency, or
  • Publish GoThru-PtGui as a Rust crate the main app depends on, or
  • Merge the source and sync periodically.

Pick an approach that lets the standalone code keep evolving without forking divergence.

Scope

  • Evaluate GoThru-PtGui structure and how it exposes stitching (CLI/lib/binary).
  • Define the integration boundary (Tauri command / sidecar / linked crate).
  • Wire stitching into the app's Edit/Stitching flow.
  • Document the update/sync process so upstream changes flow in.

Acceptance Criteria

  1. Stitching from GoThru-PtGui is invocable inside the main Photo Studio app.
  2. A documented, low-friction path exists to pull in upstream GoThru-PtGui updates.
  3. Stitching runs end-to-end on real 360 input within the app.

Related: watermarking for non-subscribers, free-during-beta, and lens-DB expansion are tracked as separate issues.

issues.display_title: Issue #115: Stitch 360: new step-by-step flow — build one 360 panorama at a time
issues.main_description_html:
Demo by developer

2026-07-24.22-09-52.mp4

Summary

Stitch 360 has been fully redesigned. It used to work in batch mode (pick one folder → process many panoramas at once). It's now a step-by-step wizard focused on building one panorama at a time — much easier to follow, including for non-technical users.

New flow (4 steps)

  1. Photos — pick the shots from a single tripod position. The photos now show up as real previews (not blank boxes).
  2. Lens — the camera & lens are auto-detected from the photos; just confirm.
  3. Stitch — runs with a progress bar.
  4. Review & fix — see the finished panorama right away. If something looks off, a guide — "something look off? tell me what you see" — points to the fix.

What's better

  • Auto camera detection — no more guessing the lens manually.
  • Real previews — both the input photos and the stitched result show on screen.
  • Fix-it guide for imperfect results (e.g. a black gap or streaky colors), in plain language instead of technical terms.
  • Cleaner UI — consistent across every step, looks good in both light and dark mode.

Notes

  • Default output size is 8K to stay safe (avoids running out of memory).
  • Some advanced options turn on automatically when the stitching engine is on the newer version.

issues.display_title: Issue #106: Full-screen modal footer is clipped in windowed mode ("Click here to learn more" cut off)
issues.main_description_html:
What happens

Upload → Upload to GoThru (and every other full-screen modal): the footer is clipped at the bottom of the window. The description line is visible, but the "Click here to learn more" link underneath it is cut off — only the top few pixels of the text render.

Reproduces in a windowed app; in OS fullscreen the footer is fine.

Root cause: HeroUI's size="full" modal hardcodes h-[100dvh] on the wrapper slot and h-[100dvh] min-h-[100dvh] on the base slot (@heroui/theme modal.js → modal tv slots). The app renders a custom 32px titlebar and offsets the modal below it via .titlebar-safe-modal-wrapper (index.css:141), which only set top: var(--menubar-h) / bottom: 0:

  1. The wrapper has an explicit height: 100dvh, so bottom: 0 is ignored — the wrapper stays a full viewport tall while starting 32px lower, spilling exactly --menubar-h past the window bottom.
  2. The base's min-h-[100dvh] beats any max-height clamp, so shrinking the child alone doesn't help either.

--menubar-h is 32px windowed and 0px in fullscreen (TitleBar.tsx:44) — which is why the bug only shows up windowed, and why the clipped strip is exactly one titlebar tall.

How to reproduce

  1. Run the app windowed (not OS fullscreen)
  2. Select an image → Upload → GoThru, log in so the full-screen upload view shows
  3. Look at the footer: "Click here to learn more" is cut off by the window bottom edge

Fix

Fixed in the working tree (not yet committed), CSS only, in src/renderer/index.css:

.titlebar-safe-modal-wrapper {
  top: var(--menubar-h, 0px) !important;
  bottom: 0 !important;
  height: calc(100dvh - var(--menubar-h, 0px)) !important;
}

.titlebar-safe-modal-wrapper > * {
  height: 100% !important;
  min-height: 0 !important;
  max-height: 100% !important;
}

Shrinks the wrapper by the titlebar height and clears the base's min-height so the modal fits inside it. One rule fixes all four full-size modals that share this wrapper — GoThru, StreetView, Panorra, and the Help modal — instead of patching each one.

Side effect (intended): the height math in GridThumbnails.tsx, GoThru/Upload.tsx, Panorra/Upload.tsx and StreetView/Publish.tsx, which measures upload-modal-wrapper / upload-modal-footer clientHeight, now reads the corrected heights.

Goal

The full-screen modal footer must be fully visible in windowed mode — the "Click here to learn more" link clickable, no content hidden behind the window edge — matching the Electron app's layout.

Test plan reference

docs/refactor/pre-merge-test-plan.md §4 — Upload group (GoThru / StreetView / Panorra) plus the Help modal.

issues.display_title: Issue #97: Image Resize distorts rotation for photos with EXIF orientation
issues.main_description_html:
What happens

Resizing a photo with EXIF orientation 6 or 8 (portrait/rotated) through Edit → Image Resize produces a distorted, wrongly-rotated output. Orientation-1 photos are unaffected.

Root cause, two parts — both in do_resize / copy_metadata in src-tauri/src/commands/image_resize.rs:

  1. Resize doesn't apply EXIF orientation before resizing. Renderer sends targetWidth/targetHeight computed from display dimensions (orientation-corrected, width/height swapped for 6/8 — see files.rs:261-265). image::ImageReader::decode() reads raw sensor-orientation pixels (the image crate does not auto-apply EXIF orientation). resize_exact(target_w, target_h, ...) then force-stretches the raw (unswapped) pixels into the swapped target dims → wrong aspect ratio.
  2. The Orientation tag "strip" was a no-op. The fix for (1) bakes the rotation into the pixels before resizing, so the copied EXIF Orientation tag must be reset to 1 afterward or a viewer re-rotates the now-correct pixels a second time. The original attempt used -Orientation-=, which does nothing for a scalar (non-List) exiftool tag with no value — verified directly against the bundled exiftool binary ("0 image files updated", tag unchanged). rotate.rs had the exact same -Orientation-= pattern (and the same latent bug) for its own EXIF-reset step.

How to reproduce

  1. Take/use a JPEG with EXIF orientation 6 or 8 (portrait shot on a phone held in landscape, etc.)
  2. Open Edit → Image Resize, resize it
  3. Compare output rotation/aspect to source — distorted vs. expected

Found while running the pre-merge test plan (docs/refactor/pre-merge-test-plan.md §4.5, row E-3 Image Resize).

Fix

Fixed in 7cc5da9:

  • image_resize.rs: apply the EXIF orientation transform to the decoded pixels (apply_orientation, same table as rotate.rs) before resize_exact.
  • image_resize.rs and rotate.rs: swap -Orientation-= → -Orientation#=1 (raw numeric assign, bypasses the PrintConv string match a plain =1 also gets wrong) when copying metadata, so the tag is actually reset instead of silently surviving.

Goal

Resize (and Rotate) should preserve/produce the correct visual orientation and aspect ratio for every EXIF orientation value, not just 1.

issues.display_title: Issue #150: Auto Level freezes the whole device on lower-spec machines
issues.main_description_html:
What happened

A client reported that their entire device freezes — not just our app — while running
Auto Level. Mouse and other programs become unresponsive too.

Reproduced internally: CPU sits at 100% during generating, but the system stays usable. So
the freeze only shows up on machines with lower specs.

Why it happens

Two separate issues that make each other worse.

1. Auto Level uses too much memory at once.

While processing, it holds two full copies of the panorama in RAM at the same time — the
original and the corrected version. The original is kept around longer than it needs to be,
well past the point where it's still used.

For a high-resolution panorama that's roughly 800 MB – 1.2 GB of RAM for a single photo.
On a machine with 8 GB, once other apps are running, the system runs out of RAM and starts
swapping to disk. That's what freezes the whole device. The 100% CPU reading is misleading —
at that point it's disk thrashing, not actual work.

2. Auto Level uses every CPU core, leaving none for the UI.

There's no limit on how many cores the processing takes. On a machine with many cores, the
UI still gets enough time to stay responsive. On a 4-core machine, nothing is left over and
the app stops responding.

The same pattern exists in the equirectangular rotate feature, so it likely has the same
problem.

Proposed fix

  1. Release the original image from memory as soon as it's no longer needed, before the
    output is encoded. Cuts peak memory roughly in half. Biggest win for the least work.
  2. Cap how many CPU cores the processing can use, always leaving one free for the UI.
    Processing gets slightly slower, but the app stays responsive — progress stays visible and
    Cancel still works. This fixes the rotate feature at the same time.
  3. Minor: a stale comment in the Auto Level code still claims it runs an external binary. It
    hasn't since the native migration — worth correcting so it doesn't mislead later.

Output quality and accuracy are unaffected. This is purely about how the work is scheduled
and how memory is held.

Not doing for now: encoding straight to disk instead of buffering in memory, and processing
the image in bands instead of allocating the full output up front. Both are bigger reworks —
revisit only if (1) and (2) turn out to be insufficient.

Still to confirm

The memory analysis is confirmed from the code. What isn't confirmed is that it's the cause
of this client's freeze specifically. Requested from them:

  • RAM and CPU core count
  • Resolution of the panorama being processed
  • Whether the Memory column in Task Manager maxes out during the freeze

After the fix: measure peak memory before/after on a large panorama, and verify the UI stays
responsive throughout.

Where to look

src-tauri/src/pano_level/ (the processing pipeline) and
src-tauri/src/commands/auto_level.rs (the queue). Detailed allocation trace with line
numbers available on request.

📄 Client-facing report sent to the client — click to expand

Non-technical version written for the client. Kept here verbatim as a record of what was
communicated, and of what we committed to.

Report: Device Slowdown / Freeze When Using Auto Level

Status: Cause identified — fix in preparation
Date: 31 July 2026

Summary

We've investigated your report about your device freezing while running the Auto Level
feature, and we've found the cause.

This is not damage to the application or to your photo files. The process runs correctly
and the results remain accurate — the issue is with how much of your computer's resources
are being used while it runs. On devices with more limited specifications, that usage
exceeds what's available, which causes the entire system to slow down.

We've already planned the fix, and it requires nothing on your end.

What Is Actually Happening

Auto Level works by loading the entire panorama into memory (RAM), analysing its tilt, and
then repositioning every single point in the image to the correct place.

Because 360° panorama photos are very large, this process requires:

1. A large amount of memory (RAM)

While running, the application needs to hold two copies of the photo in memory at the
same time: the original and the corrected version. For a high-resolution panorama, this can
consume roughly 800 MB to 1.2 GB of RAM for a single photo.

When the available RAM runs out, the operating system starts moving data to the hard disk as
backup memory. That process is far slower — and it's what makes the entire device, not
just our application, feel frozen.

2. Every processor (CPU) core

To keep processing fast, Auto Level currently uses all available processor cores. On a
computer with many cores this is fine — there's still spare capacity left to run the
application's interface. But on a computer with fewer cores, there's no spare capacity at
all, so the interface stops responding while the process runs.

Why It Doesn't Happen on Every Device

We tested this on our internal devices and the process ran normally — CPU usage did reach
100%, but the system stayed responsive.

The difference comes down to device specifications:

Higher-spec device Lower-spec device
RAM Enough to hold two copies of the photo Not enough → system falls back to the hard disk → drastic slowdown
CPU cores Spare capacity left for the interface Fully consumed → application stops responding
Result Feels heavy but keeps running Feels like a complete freeze

So the symptoms you're experiencing are an expected outcome — and something we can fully
address from the application side.

The Planned Fix

We've prepared two main improvements:

Fix 1 — Significantly reduce memory usage

We'll change the process so that the original copy of the photo is released from memory
earlier, as soon as it's no longer needed. The effect: peak RAM usage drops by roughly
half.

This is the change that matters most for devices with limited RAM.

Fix 2 — Reserve processor capacity for the interface

We'll limit how many processor cores are used, so there's always capacity left to run the
application's interface. Processing may take slightly longer, but the application will
stay responsive throughout — you'll still be able to see progress, cancel the process, or
switch between menus.

This improvement will also apply to other features with a similar processing pattern.

What won't change: the quality and accuracy of Auto Level's results stay exactly the
same. These changes only affect how the application manages resource usage, not how it
corrects your photos.

What You Can Do In The Meantime

While waiting for the update, these steps should help:

  1. Close other applications before running Auto Level — especially your browser, as
    browsers typically consume the most RAM.
  2. Process in smaller batches — add a few photos per queue rather than dozens at once.
  3. Let the process run undisturbed — avoid force-closing the application when it appears
    frozen. In many cases the process is still running and will finish on its own.
  4. Reduce photo resolution where possible — the larger the panorama, the more memory it
    requires.

Information We Need From You

To make sure our fix actually resolves the problem on your device — rather than solving a
different one — we'd appreciate the following information:

  1. Device specifications: RAM capacity and processor type
    (Windows: right-click Start → System)
  2. Resolution of the panorama photo being processed when the freeze occurred
    (for example: 16000 × 8000 pixels)
  3. Number of photos in the queue when the problem appeared
  4. Conditions during the freeze: did only our application stop responding, or did the
    entire device freeze as well (mouse cursor stuttering too)?
  5. If possible: open Task Manager while the process is running, and note whether the
    figure in the Memory column climbs close to its maximum.

Items 1, 2, and 5 are the most helpful to us.

Next Steps

  1. We receive your device information
  2. We complete and test both fixes described above
  3. We re-test under conditions resembling your device
  4. The fix is released through an application update

We'll notify you as soon as the update is ready. If you have any questions, or notice any
other symptoms, please let us know.

Thank you for the report — reports like this genuinely help us improve the application for
all our users.
